opus-5.5.text:
I think it's less of a trade-off than people often frame it. Simulation and real data are good at different things, and the question is really which parts of the problem each one should cover.

Simulation's biggest strength is scale and safety. In locomotion, for example, you can run thousands of robots in parallel, let them fall millions of times, and never break hardware. For tasks where the physics is reasonably well understood, like rigid-body dynamics, contacts with the ground, or balancing, simulation has worked remarkably well. Much of the progress in legged robots over the past several years came from training in sim and transferring to the real robot with techniques like domain randomization, better actuator models, and system identification.

But simulation has a ceiling. The sim-to-real gap is not only about physics parameters. It's also about the diversity of the world. A simulator only contains what someone built into it. Once you move to manipulation in homes or offices, with deformable objects, liquids, clutter, and the long tail of everyday objects and situations, it becomes very hard to model everything faithfully. Building those environments also takes a lot of human engineering, so the "free scale" of simulation stops being free.

Real data is the opposite. It's expensive, slow, and hard to scale, but it's grounded. It captures the messiness and diversity of reality that we don't know how to simulate. And with large foundation models, we've seen that real-world data, especially when combined with internet-scale vision and language data, gives you generalization to semantics and new objects that simulation alone hasn't delivered.

So my view is that it's a spectrum. For low-level, physics-heavy skills like locomotion, agile motion, and dexterous control, simulation is still extremely valuable, maybe dominant. For high-level understanding and open-world manipulation, real data and web data matter more. The interesting frontier is in the middle: using real data to make simulators better, using generative models or learned world models as a kind of "data-driven simulator," and mixing both in training so each covers the other's blind spots.

In the long run I'm optimistic that the line will blur. If world models become good enough, simulation will become something learned from real data rather than hand-built, and at that point the old sim-versus-real debate turns into a question of how best to use all the data we have.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulation’s value and mentions transfer techniques, but does not say that using simulation data to advance robotics requires foundational research.

r002.rationale: It says real data is expensive, slow, and hard to scale, but does not attribute a ceiling on improvement to a finite amount of available real-world data.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've spent a lot of my career on, and my honest answer is that I don't think of it as a trade-off anymore. I think of it as a question of which data gets you which thing.

Simulation gives you scale and safety. When we were doing legged locomotion work, we could run thousands of robots in parallel, fall over millions of times, try things that would physically break a real robot, and it costs nothing. That's how you get a policy that's explored a huge space of situations. You can't get that volume of experience in the real world. A real robot might give you a few hours of useful data a day, if nothing breaks, and something usually breaks.

But simulation lies to you. It lies about contact, about friction, about motor dynamics, about the little delays and the sensor noise and the way a cable tugs on a joint. The sim-to-real gap is real, and for a long time the whole game was figuring out how to make the simulation lie less, or how to make the policy not care that it's being lied to. Domain randomization, system identification, learning residual dynamics, all of that was essentially trying to recover from the fact that sim is an approximation.

What real data gives you is ground truth. It's the only thing that actually tells you what the world does. Even a small amount of it is enormously valuable because it anchors everything. A little real data can calibrate your simulator, or fine-tune a policy that was mostly trained in sim, and that's often where the big jump in performance comes from.

So the way I think about it now, especially in the era of large models, is that these two sources are complementary and you should be greedy about both. Simulation for breadth and for anything dangerous or rare. Real data for correctness and for the things that are genuinely hard to model, like deformable objects, or liquids, or the texture of a human environment.

The thing that's changed my thinking recently is that the balance depends a lot on the task. For locomotion, sim is very good now, and you can go almost entirely sim to real. For manipulation, especially contact-rich manipulation, the physics are much harder, and real data matters a lot more. And then for the semantic parts, understanding what an object is, what a person wants, internet-scale data from video and language ends up being a third source that's not really either of those.

So if someone asks me which one wins, I'd say neither. The teams that are doing well are the ones that figure out the right mix for their problem, and then build the pipeline so that real data keeps improving the simulator and the simulator keeps generating more useful experience. It's a loop, not a choice.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation’s scale and limitations but does not state that advancing robotics with simulation still requires foundational research.

r002.rationale: It says real robots provide limited daily experience, but does not connect finite data availability to an eventual ceiling on improvement from scaling real-world data.

astra-6.text:
I see them as complementary. Simulation gives you scale: you can collect a lot of experience in parallel, explore different environments, and let the robot fail without damaging hardware. That’s especially valuable for reinforcement learning, where learning a skill can require a huge number of trials.

But the question is whether what you learn transfers to the real world. A simulator always makes approximations. Contact, friction, actuator behavior—those details can matter a lot. If your policy learns to exploit something that only exists in the simulator, more simulation data won’t necessarily help.

Real data helps you identify those gaps. You can use it to improve the simulator, to fine-tune the policy, and to test whether you’re actually making progress. It’s more expensive to collect, so I would use it where it provides the most information.

So I wouldn’t frame the goal as choosing simulation or reality. I’d build a loop: learn in simulation, test on the robot, understand what fails, and bring that information back into training. The right balance depends on the task and how well you can simulate the things that matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation’s limits and a simulation-to-robot feedback loop, but does not say that advancing robotics with simulation data still requires foundational research.

r002.rationale: It says real data is more expensive and simulation data may not help if a policy exploits simulator artifacts. It does not attribute a ceiling on scaling real-world data improvements to the finite amount of data available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simulation and real-world data play complementary roles. In simulation, you can collect a lot of data in parallel, try things that would be dangerous on a real robot, and iterate quickly. That’s especially valuable for reinforcement learning, where learning a skill can require a huge amount of trial and error.

The challenge is that a robot can exploit inaccuracies in the simulator. Contact, friction, actuator behavior—these are difficult to model perfectly. So a policy that works very well in simulation may fail on the real hardware.

Real-world data helps you understand those gaps. You can use it to improve the simulator, identify the robot’s dynamics, or fine-tune the policy. But collecting that data is slower and more expensive, and you have to think about safety and hardware wear.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one over the other. I would use simulation for the bulk of exploration and training, then use real-world experience to validate the policy and correct the discrepancies that actually matter. The goal is to make each hour of real robot experience as useful as possible.
